en: One Scroll of the Ritual Manual for Vajraśekhara Yoga Homa. Compiled by the Duke of Sui,
Grand Master of the Court with Rank Equal to the Three Dukes, Special Advancement, Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial,
Recipient of Three Thousand Households of Feudal Land, Invested with Purple Robes, Posthumously Honored as Minister of Works, and Entitled "Great Mirror" (Dajian).
I shall now explain the homa; through this, one swiftly attains accomplishment.
By means of the ritual procedures for homa, performed continuously and in accordance with the appropriate mantra, all such matters should be carried out accordingly.
Performing homa according to the respective classes brings about unsurpassed accomplishment.
Homa is said to be of many kinds; briefly stated, there are five categories.
A detailed explanation is found in the Mahāyoga, as taught in the Secret Teachings.
I shall now briefly explain the play of the Vidyādharas;
through the ritual of homa, one achieves accomplishment in the family maṇḍala.
Regarding the five matters of homa, each has many varieties.
Pacifying and increasing, the third is subjugating,
summoning is the fourth, and the fifth is magnetizing;
among these five types of homa, magnetizing is the most excellent.
I shall now explain the *muñja* grass ritual according to its application in yoga:
for the rite of pacification (*śānti*), the hearth should be perfectly circular; it should be made thus.
For the rite of increase (*puṣṭi*), it should be square; for the rite of subjugation (*abhicāra*), it should be triangular.
The Vajra-mudrā is supreme for summoning;
the long-formed Lotus is the appropriate gesture for endearment.
These five types have been explained; the mudrās are unsurpassed in their activities.

The rite for pacifying should be performed during the first watch of the night; the rite for increasing should be performed during the first part of the day, and the rite for subduing should be performed during the middle part of the day.
For the fierce methods of summoning, one may act at all times; for the rite of magnetizing, one should act during the final watch of the night.
Through these five yogas, one performs the activities while in meditative equipoise (*samāhita*).
Facing north, one performs the rite of pacification; facing east, the rite of increase;
facing south, the rite of subjugation; and one should remain facing west for the rite of wrath.
Gazing upward toward all directions is the ritual for summoning;
if performing the rite of magnetizing, one should face west.
For pacifying, one forms the Buddha-mudrā; for increasing, the jewel insignia.
The Vajra Wrath brings subjugation; the Vajra Hook performs summoning.
When the great summoning is in resonance, the Lotus Family is revered and loved.
Through these five yogas, one should perform the rite of homa.
For the rite of pacification, burn sweet wood; for increase, use fruit-bearing wood;
for subjugation, use bitter wood; for summoning, use thorny wood;
for magnetizing, use flowering wood. These are the five kinds of wood.
The practitioner should employ [the following]:
for enrichment, a three-pronged vajra; for subjugation, one should fashion a single-pronged [vajra];
for summoning, one should fashion a hook; for magnetizing, one should fashion a lotus.
The hearth for pacifying (śāntika) should be measured as one full cubit in width and half a cubit in height;
for increasing (pauṣṭika), it should be two cubits in width and half a cubit in height;
for subjugating (abhicāruka), it should have the form of a khaṭvāṅga, being triangular with each side measuring one cubit.
The vertical measurement should be half of that; for summoning, it is one cubit long, with both the horizontal and vertical dimensions reduced by half.
For attraction, it is also one cubit, with the horizontal and vertical dimensions being the same as those for summoning.
One should draw it in three tiers: in the central court, a *karmavajra*, with lotus petals drawn in the four corners;
in the second court, the four mudrās, namely the four *pāramitās*;
and in the four corners of the inner [court], offerings.
In the third court, one should paint the retinues of the deities of the eight directions;
at the four corners and the four gates, one should place the four outer offerings of the *saṃgrahavastus*.
In the center is established the Honored One Samantaprabha; this is the *kuṇḍa* for pacifying calamities.
The remaining four armies have the *caitya* as their mark; all three enclosures are thus.
In the central enclosure, one should increase [the design] by painting the *karmavajra*;
at the four corners, paint lotus petals. In the second enclosure, one should paint:
The retinue of Ratnasaṃbhava Buddha, as well as the third enclosure and its gates,
are also as previously described.
A single-pronged *karmavajra* is depicted in the four corners, with lotus petals drawn there.
In the second court, one should paint the retinue of Trailokyavijaya with the four types of wrathful forms;
the third court and the gates are also as previously described, all of them in wrathful form.
In the central court, one should draw a vajra-hook for summoning;
in the four corners, lotuses should be drawn. In the second court, the retinue of Akṣobhya Buddha should be painted;
in the four corners of the third court, [the same applies].
In the eight directions and at the four gates, as in the first *muṇḍaka*, one should show respect;
in the central court, paint the lotus of *karma*.
In the four corners, paint three-pronged vajras; these should be painted in the second court.
The retinue of Amitāyus should be depicted as four honored ones;
in the fourth corners of the third enclosure, as well as the eight directions and the four gates,
they are described in the same manner as before.
These are the five homas taught in the Yoga Tantras, which the practitioner should know.
The four mudrās and the four means of attraction, along with the eight inner and outer offerings, are arranged within the positions of the maṇḍala; the ācārya now explains them.
The practitioner sits facing south; Vajra should be in the south,
Ratna in the west, Dharma-mudrā facing north,
Karma in the east, and Lāsyā in the southwest corner.
The garland [offering] should be at the northwest corner; the place for song and mantra is in the northeast;
the mudrā of dance is in the southeast; the burning of incense is like playful sport;
the flower offering follows the direction of the garland; and the lamp should be as in the singing.
The scented ointment is like the position for a dance; the hook is behind the vajra;
the noose faces the ratna family; the chain should follow the dharma mudrā;
and the bell is known to be like karma. These follow the practitioner in a clockwise direction.
All the maṇḍalas should be established in this manner, arranged in a circular fashion.
In the second courtyard for the rite of pacification (śāntika), there are the mudrās of the four pāramitās:
the vajra trident, and the jewel-mudrā in the shape of a gem.
The Dharma [Mudrā] is like a single-pronged vajra, with a blossoming lotus atop it;
the Karma [Mudrā] is a karma-vajra; the Lāsya [Mudrā] is a three-pronged vajra;
the Mālā [Mudrā] is shaped like a jeweled crown; and the Gīta [Mudrā] should be depicted as a vīṇā lute.
Perform the single-pronged *karma*-mudrā;
the hook is the Vajra-hook, and the noose has the form of a coiled rope with one end and a half-prong at its center.
The chain is like two rings joined together.
Among them, the linked rings represent [the chain], the bells are made as vajra-bells,
the lamps take the form of wax candles, the unguents are depicted as incense burners,
the burning incense is represented by an incense burner, and the scattered flowers are made into flower trays.
In the second enclosure, one increases [the offerings] for the retinue of the Honored One Ratnasambhava;
his radiant marks are like the form of the sun, and his smile is like three prongs laid horizontally with teeth set between them;
his banner is like a precious banner standing upright.
The four wrathful deities are subdued; the *sattva* [vajra] is a three-pronged trident.
The King holds two hooks together; "Excellent!"—with both hands joined, he makes the gesture of snapping the fingers.
The Loving One holds a bow and arrow upright.
The hook-summoning of the second court is also like that of the subjugation mandala,
without any increase or decrease.
The retinue of Amitāyus consists of Dharmatā and Dharmapālā.
The *śakti* should be in the shape of a sword; for speech, one should depict the mark of a tongue.
Because it takes the form of a solar disc, within it is a single-pronged *karma*-vajra.
For extending life, it is like the *puṣṭi* rite; outside the hearth, one draws armor.
Like the shape of a person wearing armor, with both sleeves hanging down;
the sleeves are like three single-pronged [prongs], below like an inverted incense burner,
above forming the shape of three peaks, like a three-pronged vajra-pestle.
The eight inner and outer offerings, as well as the four guardians and the rest—
all the hearths are identical.
Each depicted mudrā sits upon a lotus flower, emitting flames of light.
The celestial retinues of the eight directions, like the various mudrās,
all follow the practitioner’s seat and arise from the east.
Śakra holds a single-pronged vajra, with silken streamers fluttering at its left and right.
The deity Agni is depicted holding a *kundikā* (water flask), with flames rising from a lotus seat;
Yama holds a double-pronged trident with a human head set upon it;
like Śakra, he has silken streamers flying [from his head]; and the Lord of Rākṣasas is depicted holding a sword.
The Fire Deity (Agni) sits like a flame;
the Water Deity (Varuṇa) is painted holding a noose with two ends like thighs;
the Wind Deity (Vāyu) holds a banner and sits upon a lotus; Vaiśravaṇa holds a staff.
The silk ribbons are tied as described above; the śirṣaka is half three-pronged, upon a lotus seat with flames of light.
The wise should understand this well, examining it with precision and without error.

The rim of the hearth is two finger-widths high and four finger-widths wide. Inside the rim, at the base of the hearth opening, it is two finger-widths wide. Within this, the ritual seal (mudrā) is two finger-widths high. The hearth is positioned close to the body; its upright neck is four finger-widths wide and two finger-widths long. Next, a horizontal section is ten finger-widths long and four finger-widths high. Then, it is fashioned into the shape of lotus petals so that the proportions are harmonious; from the top of the upright neck to the tips of the petals, the total length is twelve finger-widths. Both the height and depth are level with the rim. These five types of hearths are all identical. The method for preparing the ground is as in the Great Maṇḍala. For the digging and consecration, one uses the mudrās of the spades and other tools: form the *vajrabandha* with both hands, join the thumbs (*aṅguṣṭha*), wisdom fingers (*jñānī*), forefingers (*tarjanī*), and ring fingers (*anāmikā*) together and extend them upward. Recite the mantra twenty-one times. The mantra is as follows: [Mantra omitted]

"Oṃ nikhaṇa vāsude saṃhā. This is the mudrā for consecrating clay, cow dung, and unguents: join the two hands in *añjali*, bend the index and middle fingers so that their second joints touch, and extend the ring and little fingers together; move the index fingers apart to form the shape of a mouth.
Recite the mantra twenty-one times: "Oṃ ā-mṛta-nābha-vaya hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. The mudrās and mantras for consecrating the five-colored powders are both as described in the *Yogatantra*.
Consecrate the clarified butter, honey, curd, milk, as well as wood, the five grains, incense, flowers, and so forth, each seven times with the mantra of Vajrakarmapāṇi Bodhisattva.

For the mudrā: with both hands, place the *tarjanī* (index) and *jyeṣṭhā* (thumb) fingers upon the *madhyamā* (middle) and *anāmikā* (ring) nails respectively; extend the remaining three fingers (*tarjanī*, *madhyamā*, and *anāmikā*) upward and apart, forming the shape of a *vajra*.

Then, interlace the fingers, pressing the right over the left. The mantra is: "Oṃ vajrakarma khaṅ. All items for the burnt offering (*homa*) should be placed on the right side. Ghee is placed upon a lotus-leaf stand; honey, curd, milk, rice porridge, and cooked rice are placed near the right side of the hearth. On the left side, place two vessels filled with scented water. For these vessels, gold, silver, copper, white porcelain, or conch shells may all be used interchangeably. For incense, use white sandalwood, *uragasāra* (turmeric), camphor, and so forth. One vessel is used for sprinkling purification water upon the fire and the offerings, while the other is used for the holy assembly and the fire deities to rinse their mouths.
For the sprinkling purification mudrā: join the thumbs and ring fingers; extend the remaining three fingers and spread them apart to form the shape of a three-pronged vajra-pestle.

Sprinkle water with this mudrā while reciting the mantra: *Oṃ amṛte hūṃ phaṭ*. For the rinsing-of-the-mouth mudrā: form a vajra-fist with the right hand, extend the index finger, and stir the water. After performing this empowerment seven times, bend the four fingers to form a hollow cup, scoop up water, lower the arm, join the palms toward the body, and sprinkle the water clockwise toward the fire.
The mantra is: "Oṃ varada-vajra-taṃ.

For the pacifying rite (*śāntika*), the tutelary deity, the fire god, the hearth, clothing, food, incense, and flowers should all be white; one should assume the auspicious posture (*bhadrapīṭha*), corresponding with a mind of loving-kindness, with both legs crossed and knees raised, the right leg pressing upon the left.
For the increasing rite (*pauṣṭika*), all should be yellow, and one should sit in the full lotus position (*paryaṅka*).
For subjugation (*abhicāra*), use black [color] and the squatting posture (*utkuṭukāsana*);
for summoning (*ākarṣaṇa*), use red and the half-lotus posture (*ardhaparyaṅka*);
for love (*vaśīkaraṇa*), the color is the same as for summoning, and one should sit in the *bhadrapīṭha* posture with one leg extended and the foot hanging down.

From the invitation based on the samaya up to the final invitation, all should follow the primary ritual method, or alternatively, follow the five types of homa, with each family’s lord manifesting the body through the five signs of accomplishment.

Having invited [the deities] and recited praises, one establishes the noble assembly through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) and surrounds the hearth. Then, having offered *argha* water, each person forms their respective *karmamudrā* and establishes themselves, displaying their respective *samaya*. One recites the *homa* mantra one hundred and eight times. Thereafter, taking a flower and empowering it three or seven times with the mantra of the Fire God (*Agnideva*), one casts it into the fire. Then, forming the mudrā of the Fire God—with the left hand grasping the wrist of the right, the palm of the right hand extended outward, the *tarjanī* (index finger) bent across the palm, and the *madhyamā* (middle finger) moving like a hook back and forth—one beckons to invite [the deity].
Having made the offering, perform the dismissal by forming the *dhyāna-mudrā* with the *prajñā-aṅguṣṭha*.
The mantra is:

"Oṃ ehi ehi mahābhūtanirvāśini vijaya-sattvamātre hīdava huṃ te mahārama-sicchi sanihito bhava agnayeha avyaya-avyayavahana ya svāhā. Having welcomed [the deity], sprinkle it three times with scented water and rinse the mouth three times. Then, using the root mantra, ladle full portions of clarified butter (*ghṛta*) three times with a large spoon and cast them into the fire. Visualize that they enter the mouth of the Fire God (*Agni*) and proceed to the heart-lotus.
The mantra for consecrating the flowers is also used here:
*Oṃ agnaye svāhā*. With this very mantra, one should cast honey, curd, milk, wood, and even incense and flowers three times using a small ladle. One should visualize the Fire Deity with four arms:

the right hand in the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya-mudrā*), the second hand holding a rosary, the left hand holding a staff (*khaṭvāṅga*), and the second [left] hand grasping a water jar (*kuṇḍikā*).
Visualize that from the heart, throughout the entire body, there flow forth immeasurable clouds of unguents, flowers, incense, food, drink, lamps, and various other offerings.
With these, make offerings to all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, Śrāvakas, and all worldly deities.
At the end of the fire-mantra, after the word *svāhā*, recite the [names of those] as appropriate.
To seek a specific objective, one should offer three ladlefuls to the full using a large ladle as an offering. Consecrate a single flower and place it at its original seat;
then, invite [the deity] out from the furnace and return it to its original seat.

Thereafter, purify the fire three times and, with the four-syllable mantra, invite the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas to each sit upon their respective seats. Offer the three libations for rinsing the mouth until they are full.
Offer three ladlefuls of clarified butter (*ghṛta*), and then again offer three ladles each of honey, curd-milk (*dadhi*), milk, and rice porridge;
furthermore, offer wood, the five grains, flowers, and incense, each three times. Visualize that these are cast into the mouth of the Honored Sage with a sincere mind.
If performing a rite for pacifying calamities (*śāntika*), one must add ten times as much oil and sesame seeds to the five grains, and use one [piece] of wood.
One hundred and eight times, or fifty-four, or twenty-one.
The mantra is:

*Oṃ sarvapāpānahaṃ vajraye svāhā*. According to some teachings, for the rite of pacification (*śāntika*), one may use the mantra of the Mother of the Family, the mantra of the Principal Deity, or the mantra of Vairocana; in each case, the word *svāhā* is added at the end, along with words expressing the aspiration for oneself and others to eliminate all calamities. With the mind focused intently upon the holy assembly within the hearth, one visualizes that from every pore of the bodies of the holy assembly, oceans of offering clouds flow forth from beyond the heart, reaching infinite worlds to make offerings to all Buddhas and to eliminate the suffering and afflictions of all three evil realms.

Having performed the homa, offer three full ladles of clarified butter to the assembly of noble beings. Then, gather the remaining grains, incense, flowers, and so forth into a single vessel and offer them to the worldly deities of the ten directions; the remaining procedures for the other hearths are the same.

If performing the rite of augmentation (*puṣṭi*), as when previously welcoming the Fire Deity, one should immediately offer the three large wooden ladles to the Noble Assembly, along with incense, flowers, and so forth, all as before. For burning non-glutinous rice, or if desiring to prolong life by burning *kubjaka* grass, the longevity hearth (*āyuṣya-kunda*) shall be like the previous hearth for augmentation, with its exterior fashioned in the shape of armor. All other offerings, such as incense and flowers, shall be as before; however, for the non-glutinous rice and *kubjaka* grass, add ten times the amount of other substances.
The *vidyā* for increase is: "Oṃ vajrapuṣṭaye svāhā.

For the *mudrā* of extending life: form two vajra-fists with both hands, extend the index and middle fingers, and hook them together at the crown of the head. Visualize one's own body as Trailokyavijaya; upon the *mudrā*, visualize Vairocana Buddha, from whose body flows divine nectar that pours into the practitioner’s body.
The mantra for prolonging life is:

*Oṃ vajrayuṣe svāhā*. Above the word *svāhā*, one may add words for the increase of the aspirations of oneself and others, or for the prolongation of life, or whatever aspiration is currently in one's mind; such words should be inserted there.

Focus the mind on the noble assembly within the hearth. Imagine that from the hearts of the noble assembly, and from every pore of their bodies, vast oceans of clouds of offerings flow forth, reaching infinite worlds to make offerings to all Buddhas. Furthermore, these lights shine upon and touch all sentient beings of the six realms and four modes of birth, causing them all to attain prosperity, nobility, and long life.

Immediately, by means of this radiance, one should visualize the rain of the seven treasures and all necessary provisions falling within one's own home; furthermore, one should visualize celestial ambrosia pouring into one's body, permeating every pore.

If performing a rite of subjugation (*abhicāra*), one should first invite the Fire God as previously described. Using either oil made from radish or mustard seeds, buffalo ghee, or *rudhira* (blood), one first offers three large ladles to the assembly of noble ones. Then, using incenseless flowers, foul-smelling flowers, *agaru* (安息香) incense, salt, poisons, and so forth—or alternatively, iron filings—one fashions the form of the target and cuts it into pieces to cast into the fire. This may also be done with mustard seeds, wax, salt, and poisons.

At the time of casting the fire, one should visualize that from outside the heart of the Fire Deity, weapons flow out from throughout his entire body and strike the opponent's body; one should further visualize both the Fire Deity and the principal deity (iṣṭadevatā) as being in wrathful form.
The mantra is:

"HŪṂ VAJRASATTVA YA PHAṬ" (with the *phaṭ* pronounced as a single syllable). Above the syllable *pha*, add the name of the [target] person; alternatively, employ the ritual method of one's own tutelary deity (*iṣṭadevatā*), or the mantra of Acala, or the mantra of Trailokyavijaya, or the six-legged mantra of Mañjuśrī.

Visualize that from within the body of the Wrathful Deity, clouds and oceans of weapons flow forth to make offerings to all the Wrathful Deities throughout the entirety of space; these very weapons then descend upon them and their homes.

If performing the rite of summoning (*ākarṣaṇa*), the invitation of the Fire God (*Agnideva*), and the wood, flowers, and other materials used should all be as prescribed for the rite of enrichment (*puṣṭi*); however, the flowers should be from thorny trees with red blossoms, or else the substances prescribed for burning in the specific ritual of one’s chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*).
The mantra is: *HŪṂ VAJRAKARṢAYA JAḤ*.

Upon the syllable *JAḤ*, append the name of the person in question. Then, visualize that from outside the heart of the deity, immeasurable vajra-hooks flow forth from his entire body, making offerings to all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and holy ones throughout the reaches of space. Visualize these hooks summoning sentient beings from the three evil realms and establishing them in the virtuous states of humans and devas. Then, with these many hooks, enter their hearts and summon them forth.

If performing the rite of magnetizing (vaśīkaraṇa), the invitation and the materials used are all the same as above; however, for the flowers, use red flowers or those items employed in the specific ritual of the chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā).
The mantra is: *HŪṂ VAJRA MUŚYA JAḤ*.

Add the name of the person [targeted] above the syllable *JAḤ*. One should then visualize flower-arrows flowing forth from the body of the Honored One (*bendewa*), pervading immeasurable worlds to make offerings to all Buddhas and sages, and to pierce the hearts of those śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas who harbor aversion, as well as the mutual resentment among those in the six realms and four modes of birth. Then, with these many arrows, one shoots that person in five locations: namely, the forehead, the two breasts, the heart, and the lower parts.
In all ritual hearths, if ghee is unavailable, milk may also be used.
If one performs empowerment from a distance, one may either write down the person's name or take their garment, focusing the mind upon it while performing the empowerment.

Having made offerings to the noble assembly, one should present three full ladles with a large ladle to the noble assembly, followed by three sprinklings and three rinsings. Then, taking a small ladle, one should perform *homā* seven times, or twice seven, or thrice seven, for the sake of all sentient beings, using the mantra for extinguishing the three evil destinies.
The mantra is:
Oṃ vajrapāṇi visphoṭaya sarvavyādhimardanī pramokṣaya sarvavyādhigaṃti vīrya.
"Oṃ sarvasattvān sarvatathāgatavajrasamaya hūṃ traṭ. With this, one respectfully sends the noble assembly back to their original seats.
Then, using the four-syllable mantra, one invites the worldly deities of the ten directions into the fire-pit.
Following the previous procedure, one performs the threefold sprinkling and rinsing, and then... [proceeds with what follows].
Take the remaining incense, flowers, the five grains, clarified butter, honey, and so forth, and cast them into the fire while reciting their respective root mantras once or three times.
At the end of each mantra, append the specific object of one's request before *svāhā*.

Then, form the mudrās for the ritual activity (*karma*) and the samaya of the noble assembly, recite praises and make aspirations, and conclude by forming the Trailokyavijaya mudrā and releasing it by rotating it counter-clockwise.
Having thus offered the boundary, proceed according to the *japa* ritual:

exit the maṇḍala and, outside the maṇḍala, spread straw, lotus leaves, or other green grasses in the eight directions. Alternatively, smear a circular altar to form ten positions; place the positions of Brahmā and Pṛthivīdevī to the right and left of Śakra, making ten together with the eight directions.

If there is no place to establish the positions outside the maṇḍala, one should instead establish a square boundary in a quiet and secluded area in front of the maṇḍala; within it, one should arrange eight positions and place two positions in the center, for the sake of Brahmā and the Earth Deity.

To provide food for the devas of the ten directions, one should use a mixed gruel—namely, rice, sesame seeds, and mung beans boiled together—making it extremely pure, fragrant, and delicious. Place this in a single vessel; at each seat, first set down a clean leaf, and distribute the food onto these leaves in succession.
First, take a pure vessel filled with scented water and pour a small amount of the scented water onto the leaves as an offering.
Next, using the ring and middle fingers of the right hand, flick a small amount of ointment as an offering.
Next, offer one flower and place it upon the seat.
Next, offer incense; light the burner before the seat and offer it to all the seats using this same single burner.
Next, take one ladle of gruel and place it upon the leaf to offer. Then, take a small wax candle or a paper candle to offer, and insert it into the gruel.

From the scented water to the candle, each is consecrated with its respective *mantra* three times. Once the offerings from water to candle are completed for each seat, proceed to the next. While offering the candles, maintain focused attention; until all seats have been served, do not allow the candles to go out. You must employ assistants or several attendants, each holding an item to assist with the service; if you attempt to manage everything yourself, the candles will certainly not last through the entire rite.
Append the words of the specific aspiration above each "svāhā.
The mantra of Śakra, Lord of the Devas in the East, is:
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ indrāya svāhā*. The mantra of Agni, the Deva of the Southeast, is:
“Namo samantabuddhānām agnaye svāhā. The mantra of Yama, the Deva of the southern direction, is:
“Namo samantabuddhānām yamāya svāhā. The mantra of the Lord of Rākṣasas in the southwestern direction is:
“Namo samantabuddhānām nairṛtye svāhā. The mantra of Varuṇa, the Deva of the western direction, is:
"Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ vāruṇāya svāhā. This is the mantra of Vāyu, the Deva of the northwest:
"Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ vāyave svāhā. This is the mantra of Vaiśravaṇa, the Deva of the north:
"Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ vaiśravaṇāya svāhā. This is the mantra of Īśāna, the Deva of the northeast:
"Namaḥ samantabuddhānām īśānāya svāhā. This is the mantra of Brahmā of the upper direction. "Namaḥ samantabuddhānām vṛṣabhāya svāhā.
This is the mantra of the Earth Deity (Pṛthivī) of the lower direction. The mantras of the seven luminaries are as follows:

*Namo samantabuddhānām arhaṃ śvārīye prapātaryuṭima ya svāhā.* The mantra of the twenty-eight lunar mansions (*nakṣatras*) is as follows: *Namo samantabuddhānām nakṣatra-niṅkha ye svāhā*. In this manner, from the east to here, the homage is identical for all.

Within the eight directions, two positions are added to correspond with the upper and lower heavens; the planets are in the east and the lunar mansions in the west. All offerings are the same, though it is also permissible to perform a separate, individual sacrifice if required.
If within the homa altar, one should establish the mind by marking each according to its respective direction, nor should a formal seat be provided.
Next, the homa ritual of the three *pāda* is explained.

Place the object to be accomplished before the vessel of clarified butter (*ghṛta*); if the object is large, place it either to the right or the left. The practitioner himself, the vessel of clarified butter, the object, the hearth (*kuṇḍa*), and the assembly of deities—these constitute the five collections, which should be established in their successive order.

Take a small ladle and fill it with clarified butter (*ghṛta*); add it to the prepared substance while reciting the mantra up to the syllable *sarva*. Immediately lift the ladle and cast it into the fire, letting it descend with the sound *ha*. Then, draw out the sound *ha* long and continuously until the ladle returns to the substance, at which point the sound *ha* finally ceases. Perform this procedure individually for each item in its entirety.
If one is performing the consecration for a person, place it upon the head of the ladle.
If the mantra of the chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā) lacks the word *svāhā*, one should add it while reciting; otherwise, proceed as previously described.
Next, the ritual procedure for the characteristics of the ladle is explained.
I shall now explain the characteristics of the pouring and the draining ladles;
by abiding in these, the practitioner will swiftly achieve accomplishment.
The ladle should be one cubit in length; made of wood according to the Dharma, it must be firm and dense, without holes or cavities.
Its mouth should be exquisitely well-formed, measuring four finger-widths across, and its depth should be one finger-width.
Its shape is like the svastika; within it, a three-pronged vajra should be made most exquisite.
Its handle’s circumference should be such that it can be grasped by a person;
near the mouth and at the end of the handle, there should be lotus patterns.
The dimensions and circularity of the ladle for pouring out, as well as its engraved carvings,
are all like those of the ladle for pouring in; the wood is also as previously described,
or one may use khadira wood, with the mouth [of the handle] made from the upper joint of a branch used for meditation.
Its circumference should be the prescribed measure, with a width of slightly more than one inch;
the depth should be half of that. Within it, one should fashion a lotus flower, or alternatively, a vajra.
The two ladles for pouring and emptying are as described by the Great Sage;
those seeking *siddhi* who practice recitation should perform them accordingly.
*Vajraśekhara-yoga-homa-vidhi*, one fascicle.
